strategies.name: 12-month momentum
strategies.what: Each month, buys the 10 stocks that rose most over the past year (skipping the last month).
strategies.idea: Winners tend to keep winning for a while because news sinks in slowly.
strategies.reason: Made more than holding (18.0% vs 15.1% a year), but with much bigger swings (worst drop -40.3% vs -25.3%). Per unit of risk it did worse (Sharpe 0.64 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: Residual momentum
strategies.what: Each month, buys the 10 stocks with the strongest rise of their own, after removing the part that came from the whole market moving.
strategies.idea: Momentum that isn't just 'the market went up' is steadier and crashes less.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but lost to it in 2018–2020 (Sharpe 0.46 vs 0.70). The win didn't repeat, so it was probably luck or one kind of market.

strategies.name: Near the 52-week high
strategies.what: Each month, buys the 10 stocks closest to their highest price of the past year.
strategies.idea: Investors hesitate to buy near a high, so good news gets priced in late.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.27 vs 0.88, 3.4% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Smooth momentum
strategies.what: Among the 30 strongest stocks of the past year, buys the 10 whose rise came in many small steps rather than a few big jumps.
strategies.idea: Slow, steady gains go unnoticed (like a frog in warming water), so they last longer.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.60 vs 0.88, 13.9% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Risk-adjusted momentum
strategies.what: Each month, buys the 10 stocks with the best past-year gain per unit of volatility.
strategies.idea: A calm rise is a more reliable signal than a wild one.
strategies.reason: Made more than holding (19.9% vs 15.1% a year), but with much bigger swings (worst drop -35.2% vs -25.3%). Per unit of risk it did worse (Sharpe 0.74 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: Volatility-managed momentum
strategies.what: 12-month momentum, but invests less money when the picks have been swinging a lot.
strategies.idea: Momentum crashes tend to come in volatile markets, so stepping back then should help.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.82 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Momentum with a bear-market switch
strategies.what: Holds the 10 strongest stocks, but after a two-year market fall switches to holding every stock.
strategies.idea: Momentum often crashes when markets rebound after a long fall.
strategies.reason: Made more than holding (17.0% vs 15.1% a year), but with much bigger swings (worst drop -40.3% vs -25.3%). Per unit of risk it did worse (Sharpe 0.62 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: Each stock vs T-bills
strategies.what: Holds every stock whose past-year gain beat what cash (T-bills) earned; the rest sits in cash.
strategies.idea: Only own what's actually going up; step aside from what isn't.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.85 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Older momentum (12 to 7 months)
strategies.what: Buys the 10 stocks that did best from 12 to 7 months ago, ignoring the last six months.
strategies.idea: Some research says the older part of the trend predicts better.
strategies.reason: Made more than holding (23.0% vs 15.1% a year), but with much bigger swings (worst drop -37.0% vs -25.3%). Per unit of risk it did worse (Sharpe 0.79 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: Momentum acceleration
strategies.what: Buys the 10 rising stocks whose last six months beat the six before by the most.
strategies.idea: A trend that's speeding up may have more to run.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.57 vs 0.88, 12.7% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Consistent momentum
strategies.what: Buys the strongest stocks of the past year, but only those that were up in at least 8 of the 11 months.
strategies.idea: Gains spread across many months are less likely to be one lucky event.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.55 vs 0.88, 12.9% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Regression momentum (Clenow)
strategies.what: Each week, ranks stocks by how steeply and smoothly they've climbed over 90 days and holds the top 10, with trend and crash filters.
strategies.idea: A popular book method: buy the cleanest uptrends, drop them when the trend breaks.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.65 vs 0.88, 12.6% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Last week's losers
strategies.what: Each Friday, buys the 10 stocks that fell most over the week, for one week.
strategies.idea: Short-term overreactions often bounce back.
strategies.reason: Before trading costs it beat holding (Sharpe 0.95 vs 0.88), but it trades its whole account about 90 times a year and the costs ate the edge (Sharpe 0.65 after them).

strategies.name: Last month's losers
strategies.what: Each month, buys the 10 stocks that fell most over the past month.
strategies.idea: Big one-month drops sometimes overshoot and recover.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.57 vs 0.88, 13.1% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Market-adjusted weekly losers
strategies.what: Each Friday, buys the 10 stocks that fell most compared with what the market alone would explain.
strategies.idea: A stock-specific drop with no market reason is more likely to reverse.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.47 vs 0.88, 9.8% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Overnight gainers
strategies.what: Buys the 10 stocks that gained most between close and next open over the past month.
strategies.idea: Overnight moves are said to reflect steady buying that continues.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.33 vs 0.88, 5.7% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Intraday losers
strategies.what: Buys the 10 stocks that lost most during trading hours (open to close) over the past month.
strategies.idea: Daytime selling is said to be noise that later reverses.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.15 vs 0.88, 0.0% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Hold only overnight
strategies.what: Buys every stock at the close and sells at the next open, every day.
strategies.idea: A famous finding: most of the market's gains came overnight. A test, not a usable strategy.
strategies.reason: Trades in and out every day (close -> next open), so it pays costs constantly. Before costs it would have beaten holding (Sharpe 0.89 vs 0.88); after them it didn't.

strategies.name: Lowest volatility
strategies.what: Each month, holds the 20 calmest stocks of the past year.
strategies.idea: Calm stocks have historically done about as well as wild ones, with smaller drops.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.88 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Low beta
strategies.what: Each month, holds the 20 stocks that move least with the market.
strategies.idea: Investors overpay for high-beta stocks, so low-beta ones are often cheap.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.81 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Low stock-specific volatility
strategies.what: Each month, holds the 20 stocks with the smallest moves of their own (not counting market moves).
strategies.idea: Stocks with big individual swings tend to be overpriced lottery tickets.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but in 2018–2020 it was only about even with holding: not clearly better, not clearly worse.

strategies.name: Skip the lottery tickets
strategies.what: Holds every stock except the 20% with the biggest single-day jump last month.
strategies.idea: Stocks that just had a huge day attract gamblers and later lag.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but lost to it in 2018–2020 (Sharpe 0.60 vs 0.70). The win didn't repeat, so it was probably luck or one kind of market.

strategies.name: Low skew
strategies.what: Each month, holds the 20 stocks with the fewest big up-spikes recently.
strategies.idea: People overpay for the chance of a big jump.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.56 vs 0.88, 8.8% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Minimum variance
strategies.what: Each month, picks the mix of stocks (max 10% each) that would have swung the least together.
strategies.idea: Combining calm, unrelated stocks gives a smoother ride.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but lost to it in 2018–2020 (Sharpe 0.55 vs 0.70). The win didn't repeat, so it was probably luck or one kind of market.

strategies.name: NR7 breakout
strategies.what: After the quietest day of the last 7, buys if the price breaks above that day's high (in an uptrend).
strategies.idea: Quiet days often come before a big move.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.10 vs 0.88, 0.1% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Squeeze breakout
strategies.what: After at least 5 days of very tight price swings, buys on the first strong push upward.
strategies.idea: Volatility comes in cycles: squeezes tend to end in a burst.
strategies.reason: Before trading costs it beat holding (Sharpe 1.05 vs 0.88), but it trades its whole account about 44 times a year and the costs ate the edge (Sharpe 0.85 after them).

strategies.name: Keltner channel trend
strategies.what: Buys when the price closes well above its recent average plus two typical daily ranges; sells below the average.
strategies.idea: A strong push out of the usual range often starts a trend.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.36 vs 0.88, 5.5% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Big-day follow-through
strategies.what: Buys after a day with an unusually wide range that closes near its high, in an uptrend.
strategies.idea: A powerful day signals buyers in control.
strategies.reason: Before trading costs it beat holding (Sharpe 1.02 vs 0.88), but it trades its whole account about 85 times a year and the costs ate the edge (Sharpe 0.70 after them).

strategies.name: Opening-range breakout
strategies.what: Buys during the day if the price rises half of yesterday's range above today's open; sells at the close.
strategies.idea: An old day-trading method (Larry Williams). Trades inside the day.
strategies.reason: Trades in and out every day (buy-stop after the open -> close), so it pays costs constantly. Even before costs it didn't beat holding (Sharpe -2.56 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: Close near the low (IBS)
strategies.what: Buys an uptrending stock that closes near the bottom of its day's range; sells when it closes near the top or after 5 days.
strategies.idea: Weak closes in strong stocks tend to bounce.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe -0.25 vs 0.88, -6.6% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Three down days
strategies.what: Buys an uptrending stock after 3 lower closes in a row; sells on the first up close.
strategies.idea: Short pullbacks in an uptrend usually don't last.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe -1.08 vs 0.88, -24.6% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Unusual drop vs the market
strategies.what: Buys when a stock has fallen unusually far over 5 days compared with the market, in an uptrend.
strategies.idea: Extreme stock-specific drops tend to snap back.
strategies.reason: Before trading costs it beat holding (Sharpe 0.99 vs 0.88), but it trades its whole account about 108 times a year and the costs ate the edge (Sharpe 0.56 after them).

strategies.name: Dips in bouncy stocks
strategies.what: Buys 10-day lows, but only in stocks that historically tend to reverse rather than trend.
strategies.idea: Buying dips works better where prices tend to bounce.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe -0.14 vs 0.88, -5.9% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Daily weakest closes
strategies.what: Every day, holds the 5 uptrending stocks that closed weakest in their day's range, for one day.
strategies.idea: Same bounce idea as IBS, as a daily basket.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe -1.17 vs 0.88, -25.9% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Deep-fall turnaround
strategies.what: Buys a stock at least 30% below its high once it climbs back above a rising 50-day average.
strategies.idea: Beaten-down stocks that start trending up again can recover strongly.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 45% of the time and earned 4.4% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Gap-up continuation
strategies.what: Buys a stock that opens 4%+ higher on heavy volume and holds its gains.
strategies.idea: Big news gaps tend to keep moving in the same direction.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.12 vs 0.88, -0.7% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Gap-down recovery
strategies.what: Buys an uptrending stock that opens 3%+ lower but closes above its open, on normal volume.
strategies.idea: A drop with no real news that recovers during the day is often a false alarm.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 48% of the time and earned 4.2% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Fade the gap down
strategies.what: Buys at the open after a 2%+ gap down in an uptrend; sells the same day at the close.
strategies.idea: Gaps often partly fill during the day. Trades inside the day.
strategies.reason: Trades in and out every day (open -> close), so it pays costs constantly. Even before costs it didn't beat holding (Sharpe -0.75 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: Big-news drift
strategies.what: Buys after an unusually large stock-specific rise on heavy volume; holds 20 days.
strategies.idea: Prices underreact to real news and keep drifting.
strategies.reason: Before trading costs it beat holding (Sharpe 1.02 vs 0.88), but it trades its whole account about 47 times a year and the costs ate the edge (Sharpe 0.81 after them).

strategies.name: Quiet-drop reversal
strategies.what: Buys after an unusually large stock-specific fall on light volume; holds 10 days.
strategies.idea: A big fall without heavy volume is more likely noise than news.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 58% of the time and earned 11.9% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Buy the crash day
strategies.what: When the market falls 3% or more in a day, buys every stock for 5 days.
strategies.idea: Panics often overshoot.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 3% of the time and earned 2.5% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Turn of the month
strategies.what: Holds stocks only around the last and first trading days of each month; cash otherwise.
strategies.idea: Paychecks and fund flows arrive at month-end.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 19% of the time and earned 2.8% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Sell in May
strategies.what: Holds stocks from November to April and cash from May to October.
strategies.idea: A centuries-old saying: winter months have historically been stronger.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 48% of the time and earned 8.3% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Same-month seasonality
strategies.what: Each month, buys the 10 stocks that did best in that calendar month over the past 5 years.
strategies.idea: Some stocks repeat seasonal patterns (earnings timing, demand cycles).
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.46 vs 0.88, 9.5% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: December tax-loss rebound
strategies.what: In mid-December, buys the 10 worst stocks of the year and holds them to the end of January.
strategies.idea: Investors dump losers for tax reasons in December; the selling stops in January.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 10% of the time and earned 3.1% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Santa Claus rally
strategies.what: Holds stocks only for the last days of December and first days of January.
strategies.idea: The holiday period has historically been strong.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but in 2018–2020 it was only about even with holding: not clearly better, not clearly worse. It was in the market only 3% of the time, so it earned 3.6% a year vs 15.1% for holding: a high Sharpe isn't the same as a high return.

strategies.name: Options expiration week
strategies.what: Holds stocks only during the week of monthly options expiration.
strategies.idea: Option hedging flows are said to push prices up that week.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 23% of the time and earned -1.6% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Skip Mondays
strategies.what: Holds stocks every day except over the weekend into Monday.
strategies.idea: Mondays have historically been the weakest day.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.04 vs 0.88, -0.6% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Quarter-end window dressing
strategies.what: Buys the quarter's 10 best stocks in its last week.
strategies.idea: Fund managers buy winners before quarter-end to look good in reports.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 8% of the time and earned 1.5% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Beta rotation
strategies.what: Holds the 20 most market-sensitive stocks when most stocks are in uptrends, the 20 least when few are.
strategies.idea: Be aggressive in strong markets and defensive in weak ones.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.40 vs 0.88, 8.0% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Breadth regime
strategies.what: Holds every stock while more than half are above their 200-day average; cash when fewer than 40% are.
strategies.idea: When most stocks are in downtrends, the market is risky.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.78 vs 0.88, 10.2% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: New highs vs new lows
strategies.what: Holds stocks while more are hitting 52-week highs than lows; cash otherwise.
strategies.idea: More new lows than highs signals a weakening market.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.44 vs 0.88, 5.5% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Breadth thrust
strategies.what: After a sudden swing from few to most stocks rising, holds every stock for 3 months.
strategies.idea: A rare signal (Zweig) that has marked the start of big rallies.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 33% of the time and earned 5.9% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Breadth washout
strategies.what: When fewer than 10% of stocks are above their 20-day average, buys every stock for a month.
strategies.idea: Extreme selling is often near a bottom.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 13% of the time and earned 7.4% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Advance/decline warning
strategies.what: Steps into cash when the market is near its high but fewer stocks are rising.
strategies.idea: A rally led by fewer and fewer stocks is fragile.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.56 vs 0.88, 7.9% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Absorption ratio
strategies.what: Steps into cash when stocks suddenly start moving together much more than usual.
strategies.idea: When everything moves as one, the market is fragile (Kritzman et al.).
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but lost to it in 2018–2020 (Sharpe -0.05 vs 0.70). The win didn't repeat, so it was probably luck or one kind of market.

strategies.name: Market turbulence
strategies.what: Steps into cash when daily moves become statistically unusual compared with the past 3 years.
strategies.idea: Unusual market behaviour often comes before big drops.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.59 vs 0.88, 8.1% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Dual momentum
strategies.what: Holds the 10 strongest stocks of the past year, but only those that also beat cash; the rest in cash.
strategies.idea: Combines 'best of the group' with 'actually going up' (Antonacci).
strategies.reason: Made more than holding (20.0% vs 15.1% a year), but with much bigger swings (worst drop -42.4% vs -25.3%). Per unit of risk it did worse (Sharpe 0.69 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: Protective momentum
strategies.what: Holds the 10 strongest stocks, moving more into cash as more stocks turn negative.
strategies.idea: Weak breadth is a warning, so reduce risk gradually.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but in 2018–2020 it was only about even with holding: not clearly better, not clearly worse. It was in the market only 35% of the time, so it earned 9.9% a year vs 15.1% for holding: a high Sharpe isn't the same as a high return.

strategies.name: Canary momentum
strategies.what: Holds the 10 strongest stocks only while both the S&P 500 and the average stock have positive momentum.
strategies.idea: Use the market as a canary in the coal mine (Keller).
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.53 vs 0.88, 12.0% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Winners on dips
strategies.what: Each Friday, buys the 5 strongest-trend stocks that fell most this week; holds 2 weeks.
strategies.idea: Buy strong stocks when they're briefly on sale.
strategies.reason: Made more than holding (19.3% vs 15.1% a year), but with much bigger swings (worst drop -31.4% vs -25.3%). Per unit of risk it did worse (Sharpe 0.68 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: Pullback in a strong trend
strategies.what: In a strong uptrend, buys after the price touches its 20-day average and then turns up.
strategies.idea: A classic swing-trading entry.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.21 vs 0.88, 2.3% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Pullback near the high
strategies.what: Buys a stock near its 52-week high after a 3%+ dip; sells at a new high or after 10 days.
strategies.idea: Strong stocks' small dips are usually bought quickly.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.22 vs 0.88, 2.5% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Trend quality
strategies.what: Buys when a stock's last 20 days moved mostly in one direction (up) above its 50-day average.
strategies.idea: Clean, efficient trends are more likely to continue than choppy ones.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.04 vs 0.88, -1.6% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Momentum with a trend exit
strategies.what: Buys the strongest stocks monthly, but sells any that close below their 100-day average.
strategies.idea: Keep the winners, cut those whose trend breaks.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.49 vs 0.88, 10.4% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Least liquid big stocks
strategies.what: Each month, holds the 20 stocks whose price moves most per dollar traded.
strategies.idea: Investors want extra return for holding harder-to-trade stocks.
strategies.reason: Made more than holding (19.1% vs 15.1% a year), but with much bigger swings (worst drop -26.1% vs -25.3%). Per unit of risk it did worse (Sharpe 0.77 vs 0.88).

strategies.name: High-volume premium
strategies.what: Each month, buys the 10 stocks whose trading volume suddenly jumped without a big price move.
strategies.idea: Unusual volume draws attention and new buyers to a stock (Gervais, Kaniel & Mingelgrin).
strategies.reason: Beat holding the same stocks in 2021–now and again in 2018–2020, years that weren't used to pick it (it beat holding in 85% of the resampled tests there).

strategies.name: Volume accumulation (OBV)
strategies.what: Buys when on-balance volume hits a new high while the price hasn't yet.
strategies.idea: Volume can lead price when big buyers are quietly accumulating.
strategies.reason: Before trading costs it beat holding (Sharpe 1.00 vs 0.88), but it trades its whole account about 64 times a year and the costs ate the edge (Sharpe 0.65 after them).

strategies.name: Money flow
strategies.what: Buys when the Chaikin money-flow indicator turns clearly positive in an uptrend.
strategies.idea: Closes near the day's high on heavy volume show buying pressure.
strategies.reason: Before trading costs it beat holding (Sharpe 0.96 vs 0.88), but it trades its whole account about 37 times a year and the costs ate the edge (Sharpe 0.75 after them).

strategies.name: Quiet pullback
strategies.what: In an uptrend, after 3 down days on light volume, buys the first up day on heavy volume.
strategies.idea: Pullbacks without heavy selling are healthy pauses.
strategies.reason: Smaller drops, but it was in the market only 59% of the time and earned 12.0% a year vs 15.1% for holding. Sitting out also meant missing the gains.

strategies.name: Correlation spike
strategies.what: Steps into cash when stocks move unusually together and the market is falling.
strategies.idea: High correlation in a falling market signals panic.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.88 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Dispersion momentum
strategies.what: Holds the 10 strongest stocks when stocks' returns differ a lot; holds every stock otherwise.
strategies.idea: Momentum works best when winners and losers really separate.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.51 vs 0.88, 11.6% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Least market-linked stocks
strategies.what: Each month, holds the 20 stocks least correlated with the market.
strategies.idea: Stocks that march to their own drum diversify a portfolio.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.77 vs 0.88, 10.8% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: First new high after a base
strategies.what: Buys a stock's first 52-week high after 3 months without one; sells below the 50-day average.
strategies.idea: Breaking out of a long base can start a new leg up.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.42 vs 0.88, 5.8% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: New top-100 entrant
strategies.what: Buys stocks that just entered the 100 biggest, holds them for a quarter.
strategies.idea: Newly big companies attract index and fund buying.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.47 vs 0.88, 9.8% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Skip stocks near their lows
strategies.what: Holds every stock except those within 5% of their 52-week low.
strategies.idea: Stocks near their lows often keep falling.
strategies.reason: Beat holding the same stocks in 2021–now and again in 2018–2020, years that weren't used to pick it (it beat holding in 83% of the resampled tests there).

strategies.name: Composite: momentum + calm + near high
strategies.what: Each month, holds the 15 stocks with the best average rank on momentum, low volatility and closeness to the 52-week high.
strategies.idea: Mixing several proven ideas spreads the risk of any one failing.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.84 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Calm stocks in uptrends
strategies.what: Each month, holds the 20 calmest stocks among those above their 200-day average.
strategies.idea: Low volatility without the falling knives.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.79 vs 0.88, 9.3% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: 5-signal trend vote
strategies.what: Holds stocks where at least 4 of 5 trend checks agree; sells when 2 or fewer do.
strategies.idea: Several signals agreeing should mean fewer false alarms.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.83 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Site line-up vote
strategies.what: Holds a stock when at least 3 of the site's own on-site strategies are holding it.
strategies.idea: If several of our strategies agree, the signal should be stronger.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but lost to it in 2018–2020 (Sharpe 0.63 vs 0.70). The win didn't repeat, so it was probably luck or one kind of market.

strategies.name: Momentum with breadth filter
strategies.what: Holds the 10 strongest stocks only while more than half of stocks are above their 200-day average.
strategies.idea: Avoid momentum's crashes in weak markets.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.27 vs 0.88, 3.6% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Factor rotation
strategies.what: Each month, switches to whichever of three styles (momentum, low volatility, near-high) did best over 6 months.
strategies.idea: Investment styles themselves have momentum.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.34 vs 0.88, 6.0% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Multi-horizon trend
strategies.what: Holds stocks that are up over 1, 3, 6 and 12 months; sells when 2 or more turn negative.
strategies.idea: A trend confirmed on every timescale is more reliable.
strategies.reason: Did worse than simply holding the same stocks: Sharpe 0.53 vs 0.88, 7.1% a year vs 15.1%.

strategies.name: Inverse-volatility weighting
strategies.what: Holds every stock, putting more money in calm ones and less in wild ones.
strategies.idea: A simple form of risk parity: each stock contributes similar risk.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but in 2018–2020 it was only about even with holding: not clearly better, not clearly worse.

strategies.name: Volatility-targeted composite
strategies.what: The composite strategy, investing less when it's been swinging more than 12% a year.
strategies.idea: Keep the ride steady by sizing down in rough patches.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.83 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Drawdown brake
strategies.what: Holds every stock, but halves the position after a 10% fall until the market makes a new 3-month high.
strategies.idea: Cut risk when losing, rebuild when the market recovers.
strategies.reason: Almost exactly the same as holding (Sharpe 0.88 vs 0.88). No real edge, just extra trading.

strategies.name: Breadth-scaled exposure
strategies.what: Invests more the larger the share of stocks above their 200-day average.
strategies.idea: Scale risk with the health of the market.
strategies.reason: Beat holding in 2021–now, but lost to it in 2018–2020 (Sharpe 0.35 vs 0.70). The win didn't repeat, so it was probably luck or one kind of market.
